candidates.title: Evaluation of tracking performance and robustness for a hybrid locomotion controller
candidates.description: Legged locomotion is a complex control problem that requires both accuracy and robustness to cope with real-world challenges. Legged systems have traditionally been controlled using trajectory optimization with inverse dynamics. Such hierarchical model-based methods are appealing due to intuitive cost function tuning, accurate planning, generalization, and most importantly, the insightful understanding gained from more than one decade of extensive research. However, model mismatch and violation of assumptions are common sources of faulty operation. Simulation-based reinforcement learning, on the other hand, results in locomotion policies with unprecedented robustness and recovery skills. Yet, all learning algorithms struggle with sparse rewards emerging from environments where valid footholds are rare, such as gaps or stepping stones. In this work, we propose a hybrid control architecture that combines the advantages of both worlds to simultaneously achieve greater robustness, foot-placement accuracy, and terrain generalization. Our approach utilizes a model-based planner to roll out a reference motion during training. A deep neural network policy is trained in simulation, aiming to track the optimized footholds. We evaluate the accuracy of our locomotion pipeline on sparse terrains, where pure data-driven methods are prone to fail. Furthermore, we demonstrate superior robustness in the presence of slippery or deformable ground when compared to model-based counterparts. Finally, we show that our proposed tracking controller generalizes across different trajectory optimization methods not seen during training. In conclusion, our work unites the predictive capabilities and optimality guarantees of online planning with the inherent robustness attributed to offline learning.

candidates.title: IMD: A 6-DoF Pose Estimation Benchmark for Industrial Metallic Objects
candidates.description: Object 6DoF (6D) pose estimation is essential for robotic perception, especially in industrial settings. It enables robots to interact with the environment and manipulate objects. However, existing benchmarks on object 6D pose estimation primarily use everyday objects with rich textures and low-reflectivity, limiting model generalization to industrial scenarios where objects are often metallic, texture-less, and highly reflective. To address this gap, we propose a novel dataset and benchmark namely Industrial Metallic Dataset (IMD), tailored for industrial applications. Our dataset comprises 45 true-to-scale industrial components, captured with an RGB-D camera under natural indoor lighting and varied object arrangements to replicate real-world conditions. The benchmark supports three tasks, including video object segmentation, 6D pose tracking, and one-shot 6D pose estimation. We evaluate existing state-of-the-art models, including XMem and SAM2 for segmentation, and BundleTrack and BundleSDF for pose estimation, to assess model performance in industrial contexts. Evaluation results show that our industrial dataset is more challenging than existing household object datasets. This benchmark provides the baseline for developing and comparing segmentation and pose estimation algorithms that better generalize to industrial robotics scenarios.

candidates.title: Code and data from: milliWatt ultrasound for navigation in visually degraded environments on palm-sized aerial robots
candidates.description: Tiny palm-sized aerial robots possess exceptional agility and cost-effectiveness in navigating confined and cluttered environments. However, their limited payload capacity directly constrains the sensing suite on board the robot, thereby limiting critical navigational tasks in GPS-denied wild scenes. Commonly used sensors for obstacle avoidance become ineffective in visually degraded conditions such as low visibility, dust, fog, or complete darkness. Inspired by bats, we propose Saranga, a low-power ultrasound-based perception stack that localizes obstacles using a dual sonar array. We present two key ideas to combat the low SNR: Physical noise reduction and a deep learning based denoising method. Firstly, we find an optimal and practical way to block propeller-induced noise. Secondly, we generate and train a neural network to denoise signals. For the first time ever, we enable a palm-sized aerial robot to navigate in visually degraded conditions with thin and transparent obstacles using only on-board sensing and computation. This repository contains the dataset and trained model for the Saranga neural network. The associated code is published as a linked Zenodo record. The contents are organized in chronological order of the pipeline: Dataset (Dryad) 1. Generated dataset used for training and evaluation. 2. Trained model checkpoints for the Saranga network.; Code (Zenodo): 1. Dataset generator script. 2. Training code for the Saranga network. 3. TensorFlow Lite quantization and Edge TPU compilation scripts for Saranga. 4. ROS2 Humble source codes for our onboard autonomy stack including drivers for ICU30201 ultrasonic sensors, perception and planning nodes, along with a MAVLink node for commanding the aerial robot. 5. Benchmark scripts to compare Saranga against classical methodologies. Detailed instructions are provided in the readme.md included in this repository.

candidates.title: Data from: Secure and secret cooperation in robot swarms
candidates.description: The importance of swarm robotics systems in both academic research and real-world applications is steadily increasing. However, to reach widespread adoption, new models that ensure the secure cooperation of large groups of robots need to be developed. This work introduces a method to encapsulate cooperative robotic missions in an authenticated data structure known as Merkle tree. With this method, operators can provide the "blueprint" of the swarm's mission without disclosing its raw data. In other words, data verification can be separated from data itself. We propose a system where robots in a swarm, to cooperate towards mission completion, have to "prove'' their integrity to their peers by exchanging cryptographic proofs. We show the implications of this approach for two different swarm robotics missions: foraging and maze formation. In both missions, swarm robots were able to cooperate and carry out sequential tasks without having explicit knowledge about the mission's high-level objectives. The results presented in this work demonstrate the feasibility of using Merkle trees as a cooperation mechanism for swarm robotics systems in both simulation and real-robot experiments, which has implications for future decentralized robotics applications where security plays a crucial role. This dataset includes all experimental data generated for this paper.

candidates.title: High-resolution deformation mapping of martensitic transformation and plasticity in superelastic Nickel-Titanium
candidates.description: Shape-memory alloys (SMAs) such as nitinol (NiTi) can recover large strains through a reversible stress- or temperature-induced martensitic transformation, but cyclic transformation degrades reversibility. Recent experimental evidence has linked this functional fatigue to the emission of dislocations from the fine martensitic microstructure that forms near the phase boundary, but the precise coupling mechanism between dislocation slip and martensitic microstructure is still widely debated. This creates a mesoscale gap in the understanding of SMAs and their fatigue: multiscale simulation is prohibitively expensive, while experimental methods that can spatially resolve fine microstructure and individual dislocations (e.g., transmission electron microscopy) cannot capture bulk mechanical behavior. In biomedical applications, understanding and modeling the mechanisms of slip localization and functional fatigue will be particularly crucial for the newest generations of ultra-high-purity nitinol, with flaw sizes below the theoretical crack length threshold. In the work to which this dataset is linked, we develop a new framework (MMICROSTRUCTURE) to reconstruct the geometrically necessary martensitic transformation and plastic slip in polycrystalline SMAs from high-resolution, full-field deformation maps. Using digital image correlation in a scanning electron microscope (SEM-DIC), we experimentally measure deformation with approximately 200 nanometer spatial resolution over a 0.5-millimeter field of view. We align this deformation data to austenite grain structure mapped via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Using the MMICROSTRUCTURE framework, we quantitatively map the activity of individual slip systems and martensitic variants in each DIC subset. We show that localized networks of coupled slip and martensitic reorientation form microstructural "bridges" that propagate transformation through clusters of poorly oriented grains. The energy dissipated during bridging may be the origin of the unusual prestrain effects in nitinol, where higher prestrains (for example, crimping of a medical device) have been correlated to increased fatigue strength. Contrary to recent theories of functional fatigue focusing on a Type II twin interface, we observe that the most intense slip localization events are coupled to the development of Type I twins with a finite width.

candidates.description: Animals that are competent reservoirs of zoonotic pathogens commonly suffer little morbidity or apparent pathology from the infections. To investigate mechanisms of this tolerance of infection, we used single-dose lipopolysaccharide (LPS) as an experimental model of inflammation and compared the four hour post-injection responses by three rodents: the cricetine rodent Peromyscus leucopus (LL stock), the white-footed deermouse and reservoir for agents of Lyme disease and other zoonoses, and the murids Mus musculus (outbred CD-1 breed), the house mouse, and Rattus norvegicus , the brown rat (Fischer strain). The data presented here are part of a follow-up study of this phenomenon that was previoiusly reported with the title "An Infection-Tolerant Mammalian Reservoir for Several Zoonotic Agents Broadly Counters the Inflammatory Effects of Endotoxin" ( https://doi.org/10.1128/mBio.00588-21) . The manuscript associated with the accompanying data of this follow-up study is in preparation. The basic experimental design (described below) is the same as for the prior study: a genome-wide RNA-seq of whole blood using reference transcript set and then an analysis for differential gene expression (DEG) between LPS-treated animals and controls for each of the species. The accompanying dataset comprises the DEGs for deermice, mice, and rats in this study. There were multiple differences in the rankings of the DEGs by lowest p value between species with the greatest number of differences between P. leucopus , which is in the familly Cricetidae, and the mice and rats, which are in the family Muridae. Overall, the deermice in the study displayed a greater anti-inflammatory response than the mice and rats in the study. candidates.title: Therapist-exoskeleton-patient interaction for gait therapy
candidates.description: Following a stroke, individuals often experience mobility and balance impairments due to weakness and loss of independent joint control in the lower limbs. Gait recovery is a primary goal of physical rehabilitation for these individuals, traditionally achieved through high-intensity training led by a physical therapist. However, the conventional approach used by physical therapists, applying manual assistance or resistance during training, can be physically demanding and limits their ability to physically interact with the patient at multiple joints simultaneously. Robotic exoskeletons have emerged as a promising solution, enabling multi-joint support, reducing therapist strain, and offering objective performance feedback. However, typical exoskeleton control strategies limit the physical therapist’s involvement and adaptability to the patient’s needs, which may hinder clinical adoption and outcomes. In this study, we introduce a novel gait rehabilitation paradigm based on physical Human-Robot-Human Interaction (pHRHI), in which a therapist and an individual post-stroke are each equipped with a lower-limb exoskeleton virtually connected at the hips and knees via spring-damper elements. This connection enables bidirectional physical interaction, allowing the therapist to guide the patient’s movement while receiving real-time haptic feedback. We evaluated this approach with eight chronic post-stroke participants using within-subject design, comparing the pHRHI-based training to conventional therapist-guided mobilization during treadmill walking. Results showed that the pHRHI condition led to greater joint range of motion, increased step length and height, elevated muscle activation compared to conventional therapy, and high levels of self-reported motivation and enjoyment. These findings suggest that pHRHI can effectively integrate robotic precision with therapist intuition, offering a promising framework for enhancing gait rehabilitation outcomes in post-stroke populations. The attached dataset includes kinematic, dynamic, and kinetic data collected during this study. It may be used to identify therapist action policies based on patient impairment and to design novel rehabilitative controllers strategies for lower-limb exoskeletons.

candidates.description: This repository contains the codebase developed for the MIT ARCLab STORM-AI Challenge 2025, focused on forecasting thermospheric orbit-averaged neutral mass density using AI/ML methods. Accurate density prediction is critical for satellite drag modeling, orbit propagation, and space situational awareness—especially during geomagnetically active periods. The approach integrates physics-informed feature engineering with state-of-the-art machine learning techniques, including: 🌡️ XGBoost-based Conditional Models for initial density estimation 🔄 TSLANet (Time Series Lightweight Adaptive Network) for 72-hour density trend forecasting ⚙️ Tools for data preprocessing, scaling, and feature extraction based on OMNI2 and ESA SWARM datasets 📊 Benchmarking against truth data using custom evaluation metrics such as OD-RMSE This repository is organized for transparency and reproducibility, and includes: Training scripts for decision tree and neural models Inference pipelines for both Phase 1 and Phase 1.2 datasets Environment setup (.yml) and dependencies Example visualizations and evaluation outputs We hope this project helps advance data-driven techniques in thermospheric modeling and supports broader applications in space weather forecasting and satellite operations.

candidates.description: This repository contains a manually curated dataset of 985 experimentally supported PD-L1 (CD274) regulatory interactions from 362 primary research articles involving cancer cells. The dataset captures regulatory relationships, intermediate regulators, protein complexes, and PD-L1 molecular target forms. It also provides materials used to benchmark three AI research tools (Claude, ChatGPT, and Elicit), including study retrieval results, prompts, expert feedback, edge extraction outputs, and evaluation results.

candidates.title: AI Training and Consulting Cost Scenario Benchmarks
candidates.description: This dataset contains 1,722 scenario rows derived from the published inputs and outputs of Paloren cost estimation tools. Each row records the page URL, input assumptions for volume, minutes per item, automation share, loaded hourly cost, build or setup cost and monthly running cost. Outputs include monthly hours returned, monthly value of time returned, estimated payback period and first-year net position. The models are illustrative and not survey averages; they use transparent assumptions to show how workflow volume, automation share and labor cost change the economics of AI adoption. The data are useful for sensitivity analysis and benchmark design.

candidates.description: Combined heat exchanger reactors for conducting simultaneous endothermic and exothermic reactions Junjie Chen Department of Energy and Power Engineering, School of Mechanical and Power Engineering, Henan Polytechnic University, 2000 Century Avenue, Jiaozuo, Henan, 454000, P.R. China Contributor: Junjie Chen, ORCID: 0000-0001-5055-4309, E-mail address: komcjj@gmail.com It has been described a process to generate a hydrogen rich gas by generating a catalytic film which is composed of layers of different catalysts. It is proposed that steam reforming of a hydrocarbon be performed by one layer and the energy for this process be supplied by a hydrocarbon oxidative process being promoted in the subsequent layer. Various hybrids of this theme are proposed. However, as the heat is supplied by an autothermal reaction, oxygen must be supplied along with the fuel stream. As well as the oxygen, associated nitrogen is present. This nitrogen acts to absorb process energy which lowers the thermal efficiency of the process as well as diluting the desired product, hydrogen. The presence of the nitrogen increases the load on downstream partial oxidation units which act to oxidize carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide. The nitrogen also reduces the streams suitability for use in fuel cells. Therefore, a reactor which can supply sufficient energy to an endothermic reaction without mixing the streams is needed. It has been described a method where parallel and discrete channels can be formed by stacking suitable plates to form a structure. The plates are then bonded together using brazing, welding or diffusion bonding techniques. It is also claimed that cast ceramic plates can be used with a suitable sealing mechanism. Catalyst can be adhered onto the wall and energy supplied or removed via conduction between subsequent channels. However, the design does not allow for catalyst replenishment nor precious metal recovery. Therefore, a reactor which affords an easy and cheap method for catalyst replacement and replenishment is required. candidates.title: Hardware-Rooted Protected Execution-Finality Using Scoped Non-Bearer Capabilities and Fail-Closed Finality Sinks
candidates.description: Detailed abstract A hardware-rooted or cryptographically enforced method and system prevent a proposed operation from producing an external effect until that exact operation is validated, bound, and admitted at a non-bypassable effectuation boundary. The proposed operation is first held as a Candidate Act in a non-effective hold state. A machine-verifiable act descriptor is established for the Candidate Act. Within a protected enforcement domain or protected enforcement path—such as a trusted execution environment, hardware security module, secure element, secure processor, SmartNIC, data-processing unit, memory controller, or other isolated circuitry—a set of machine-verifiable authority predicates is evaluated from the descriptor. A corresponding protected-state operation is performed, producing or referencing a protected-state representation. Protected validation evidence recording at least the predicate-validation outcome and the protected-state condition is committed before, or atomically with, authorization of a scoped non-bearer capability. The scoped non-bearer capability is cryptographically or machine-verifiably bound to the Candidate Act, the act descriptor or a digest thereof, the committed validation evidence, the protected-state representation, the execution-finality boundary, an applicable Finality Sink, a freshness constraint, and a permitted effectuation scope. Possession of the capability alone is insufficient: it is not a bearer token, API key, OAuth token, session cookie, or transferable credential. A copied, replayed, substituted, or re-presented instance fails when used for a different act, digest, sink, nonce, policy epoch, protected state, or scope. At or before the execution-finality boundary, the Finality Sink performs a machine-enforced capability-validity check and permits the Candidate Act to become externally effective only when the capability is validly bound to all required elements. Otherwise the system fails closed and the Candidate Act remains non-effective. The Finality Sink may be implemented as a network-interface egress path, memory-commit or DMA interface, accelerator-egress or tensor-egress gate, RF or optical transmit chain, actuator or motor-control interface, settlement switch, fabric switch, CXL/UCIe transaction admission point, or other hardware-controlled effectuation latch. Dependent embodiments apply the same finality sequence to purpose-bound and tenant-bound computation (Data Control Objects, Computational Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints, runtime behavioral descriptors, Linked Act Verification Records), offline CBDC spend-state consumption, cross-border payment compliance, dual-receipt privacy with sealed lawful-resolution material, AI accelerator tensor and KV-cache egress, agentic tool-calls, radio and ISAC telemetry, satellite and non-terrestrial links, robotic actuation, chiplet and photonic I/O, CXL memory-pool admission, and heterogeneous mesh-fabric transfers. Technical effect: computation, recommendation, or token possession is structurally insufficient to cause settlement, emission, actuation, memory coherency, model egress, or other external consequence. Industry-standard keywords Security architecturetrusted execution environment (TEE); confidential computing; hardware root of trust (HRoT); hardware security module (HSM); secure element; secure enclave; remote attestation; measured boot; reference monitor; complete mediation; capability-based security; least privilege; fail-closed; fail-safe; zero trust; policy enforcement point (PEP); policy decision point (PDP); split-trust; compartment isolation Authorization artifactsnon-bearer capability; act-bound capability; scoped capability; capability token; proof-of-possession; sender-constrained token; audience-restricted token; single-use authorization; nonce; freshness; anti-replay; revocation epoch; policy epoch; monotonic counter; capability consumption; burn-in latch Memory, I/O, and fabricIOMMU; SMMU; DMA remapping; RDMA memory key; PASID; VMID; CXL; CXL Type-3 memory pool; UCIe; chiplet interconnect; cache coherency (MESI/MOESI); coherency directory; memory aperture; poison / RAS; SmartNIC; DPU; SuperNIC; line-rate packet processing AI / acceleratortensor egress; KV-cache; mixture-of-experts (MoE); expert routing; GPU fabric; HBM; MIG partition; transformer engine; distillation / model extraction; runtime behavioral descriptor; algorithmic logic fingerprint (ALF); purpose binding; tenant isolation; confidential GPU Payments and regulated systemscentral bank digital currency (CBDC); offline double-spend prevention; sealed spend state; travel rule; AML/CFT; sanctions screening; dual-receipt privacy; lawful-resolution unsealing; settlement finality Telecom / RF / space6G; AI-RAN; O-RAN xApp/rApp; E2/A1/O1; ISAC; NTN; gNB scheduler; UPF; network slice; beamforming; RIS; sub-THz; optical inter-satellite link; LEO-PNT; sovereign jurisdiction token Cyber-physicalsafety interlock; actuator latch; motion envelope; sim-to-real clamping; emergency-stop dominance From an engineering-language perspective, Claims 1 and 2 describe a recognizable security and control architecture, but they use several architecture-specific labels—especially Candidate Act, Finality Sink, execution-finality boundary, protected validation evidence, and execution finality—instead of terminology that an ordinary cloud, hardware, networking, control-system, or cybersecurity engineer would normally search for. Claim 1 is essentially the method/state-machine version of the architecture. Claim 2 is substantially the same architecture expressed as components and responsibilities. The Overall Claim in Ordinary Engineering Language At the highest level, the claims state: Do not allow a proposed side-effecting operation to happen immediately. Stage it first, describe exactly what is about to happen, verify authorization and protected state in a trusted environment, create protected evidence of that validation, issue an act-specific non-transferable authorization artifact, and then require the component that actually controls the side effect to verify that artifact immediately before allowing the side effect. If anything is missing, stale, replayed, changed, or unverifiable, do nothing. The functional flow is: Proposed operation→ stage / hold it→ canonicalize exact operation parameters→ evaluate authorization conditions→ read/update protected security state→ commit protected decision evidence→ create act-specific capability→ verify capability at actual side-effect boundary→ commit/send/actuate only if verification succeeds That is the engineering meaning underneath the terminology. Translation of the Important Terms Claim terminology How standard is the wording? Conventional industry terminology What it actually means protected execution-finality Largely architecture-specific final enforcement, transactional authorization, side-effect gating, commit authorization, reference-monitor enforcement An operation does not become consequential merely because software computed or authorized it. A final enforcement mechanism decides whether the consequence may actually occur. proposed operation Standard request, command, transaction, operation, action Whatever the system seeks to do: SEND a file, write storage, transmit RF, move a motor, make a payment, expose data, etc. Candidate Act Specialized/coined label pending operation, transaction intent, staged command, proposed request, prepared operation The exact operation that is proposed but has not yet been allowed to produce its consequence. non-effective hold state Descriptive but nonstandard pending state, staged state, pre-commit state, prepare state, quarantine, blocked command state The Candidate Act exists inside the system but cannot yet cause the network send, storage commit, actuator movement, payment, etc. execution-finality boundary Specialized commit boundary, side-effect boundary, irreversible-operation boundary, actuation boundary, egress boundary The logical or physical point where an operation changes from merely proposed or computed into something that actually changes the outside world or persistent system state. machine-verifiable act descriptor Specialized compound expression canonical request representation, command envelope, transaction descriptor, operation manifest, canonical parameter set A deterministic machine-readable description of exactly what is about to happen. machine-verifiable authority predicates Partly conventional authorization predicates, access-control conditions, ABAC rules, policy conditions, authorization constraints Boolean or security conditions that must hold before the operation can proceed. protected enforcement domain Fairly conventional concept TEE, secure enclave, HSM, secure element, trusted computing base, isolated reference monitor A trusted or isolated environment in which security-critical validation occurs so ordinary application code cannot simply rewrite the decision. protected enforcement path Specialized expression for standard concept trusted execution path, secure enforcement path, mediation path, trusted I/O path A protected chain through which the security decision and its enforcement travel. protected-state operation Specialized wording secure state lookup/update, trusted counter operation, policy-state lookup, anti-replay update, quota check Reading or modifying security-sensitive state that ordinary untrusted software should not be able to forge. applicable protected-state representation Specialized state snapshot, policy-state version, epoch, counter state, security-state digest, protected record The particular protected state against which the operation was validated. protected validation evidence Specialized authorization decision record, signed decision evidence, attestation evidence, tamper-evident audit record Protected evidence showing what was checked and what the relevant protected state was when the authorization decision occurred. committed evidence Standard distributed-systems concept durable record, append-only audit entry, transaction commit The validation result is made durable or integrity-protected before the operation is allowed to proceed. scoped non-bearer capability Specialized combination of established concepts sender-constrained capability, proof-of-possession token, object capability, transaction-specific authorization token A machine-verifiable authorization artifact that is useful only for the exact permitted operation and cannot be exercised merely because somebody copied the token. cryptographically bound Standard signed binding, MAC binding, hash binding, authenticated association Cryptography connects the authorization artifact to specific parameters so they cannot be substituted afterward. freshness constraint Standard security concept nonce, timestamp, validity interval, sequence number, monotonic counter, epoch Prevents an old authorization artifact from being reused later. permitted effectuation scope Specialized wording authorization scope, action/resource constraints, transaction scope Defines precisely which consequence the authorization artifact is allowed to cause. Finality Sink Strongly architecture-specific/coined policy enforcement point, reference monitor, command gate, actuation gate, commit gate, egress gate, safety interlock The component controlling the last practical point before the consequence occurs. machine-enforced capability-validity check Descriptive token verification, capability verification, PoP verification, authorization enforcement The Finality Sink independently checks that the authorization artifact is valid before releasing the operation. external effectuation Specialized side effect, output commit, egress, transmission, actuation, externally observable state transition The moment the proposed operation actually causes a consequence. fail closed Fully standard security term default deny, fail secure If verification fails or cannot be completed, the consequence is prevented. replayed Fully standard replay attack An earlier valid authorization or operation is reused. exhausted Somewhat specialized in this context consumed capability, spent nonce, used-once authorization, quota exhausted The authorization was single-use or limited-use and has already been consumed. indeterminate Standard policy/security concept decision unavailable, PDP indeterminate, unverifiable state The system cannot reliably determine whether authorization is valid. The claim requires denial rather than guessing. 1. Candidate Act A Candidate Act is: A fully or sufficiently specified operation that the system intends to perform, but which has not yet been permitted to create its actual consequence. Suppose an AI agent determines that a file should be sent: SEND file financial-report.pdf to partner.example.com An ordinary system may operate approximately as follows: AI decision → API call → network stack → SEND Under the architecture: AI decision→ construct SEND(file_hash=X, destination=partner.example.com, protocol=HTTPS, account=A...) → hold that exact operation as the Candidate Act The operation can therefore be inspected, validated, and bound to authorization before packets actually leave the controlled boundary. In conventional terminology: Candidate Act ≈ staged command / pending transaction / transaction intent / prepared operation. The usefulness of the terminology is that a conventional word such as “request” can sometimes refer to something already transmitted or submitted. Candidate Act expressly identifies a state in which: the operation exists, but its consequence does not yet exist. 2. Non-Effective Hold State The non-effective hold state is the state in which the Candidate Act remains before release. It means: The operation has been computed or prepared, but some mechanism prevents it from yet producing the protected consequence. This resembles the prepare stage in transactional systems. For example: Database UPDATE balance ... The update may have been constructed but is not yet committed. Network A message may have been constructed in memory but not yet transmitted through the NIC. Robot MOVE_ARM(x=20,y=15) The command may have been generated, but the motor-control signal remains inhibited. Accordingly: non-effective hold state ≈ staged / prepared / pre-commit / interlocked state. 3. Execution-Finality Boundary The execution-finality boundary identifies the point separating: something the computer intends to do from something that has actually become consequential. The specific boundary varies by technology. Domain Possible execution-finality boundary Network NIC/DPU transmission or egress Storage persistent write or commit Memory protected memory commit GPU/NPU accelerator output or egress Payment ledger or value-transfer commit Telecom RF transmission Satellite command or actuator interface Robot motor or actuator controller Power system switching or enable interface Data disclosure interface that actually releases protected bytes In conventional systems literature, this may be called the: side-effect boundary, commit point, actuation boundary, egress boundary, or irreversible-operation boundary. The claim generalizes those domain-specific boundaries under a common architectural concept. 4. Finality Sink The Finality Sink is not simply another authorization server. It is the enforcement component controlling the actual consequence. In ordinary industry terminology, depending on the implementation, it may correspond functionally to a: reference monitorpolicy enforcement point (PEP)command gateactuation gatetransaction commit gateegress enforcement pointsafety interlock An important additional condition in the claim is that the Finality Sink must be positioned at or before the execution-finality boundary and must control whether the operation crosses that boundary. That positioning is significant. Consider: Authorization server → AI agent → application → OS → driver → NIC Checking authorization only near the beginning of this chain does not necessarily prove that the same operation eventually reached the NIC unchanged. The claim instead requires a structure effectively resembling: Authorization and protected state↓bound capability↓application↓OS/driver↓ Finality Sink ↓NIC transmission The Finality Sink effectively determines: “Is the exact operation about to be released the same operation that was authorized under the relevant protected state?” That is a more precise functional interpretation of Finality Sink than merely describing it as a policy enforcement point. 5. Machine-Verifiable Act Descriptor The machine-verifiable act descriptor answers: Exactly what operation is being authorized? For a SEND operation, it might represent: operation = SEND source = account-A object_digest = 75AE... destination = partner.example.com protocol = HTTPS purpose = regulatory-report maximum_bytes = 8MB expiry = T The actual encoding may use CBOR, JSON, Protocol Buffers, a canonical binary structure, a digest tree, or another deterministic representation. The important requirement is not the particular format. The important requirement is that the representation be deterministic enough for machines to compare what was authorized with what is actually about to happen. Conventional terminology includes: canonicalized request,transaction descriptor,command envelope,signed request parameters, oroperation manifest. 6. Authority Predicates A predicate is essentially a condition that evaluates to true or false. The claim refers to a: “set of machine-verifiable authority predicates” Such conditions may include: user_role == administrator AND operation == SEND AND destination == approved_destination AND file_classification 0 This corresponds to familiar concepts such as: RBAC conditions,ABAC predicates,policy rules,authorization constraints, orpolicy-decision logic. The wording is broader because authority does not necessarily have to originate from a conventional IAM system. 7. Protected Enforcement Domain The protected enforcement domain is a trusted or isolated environment in which security-critical validation occurs so that ordinary application code cannot freely manipulate the validation process or outcome. Claim 2 expressly provides examples such as: secure processor,trusted execution environment (TEE),hardware security module (HSM),secure element,programmable network interface,data-processing unit (DPU),protected controller, etc. Functionally: Protected Enforcement Domain ≈ isolated trusted computing environment containing critical reference-monitor or policy-enforcement logic. Possible implementations include: Intel TDX/SGX-like environmentsARM TrustZone-type environmentsHSMssmart NICs / DPUssecure elementsmicrocontroller protection domainsisolated hypervisor components The claim therefore does not depend upon one particular vendor implementation. 8. Protected-State Operation The architecture does not rely only on static credentials or static authorization. The protected domain may also read or modify security-sensitive mutable state. Examples include: revocation generationnonce stateanti-replay countersingle-use stateremaining quotacurrent policy versioncurrent authorization epochdevice operating state For example: capability_generation = 47 current_generation = 48 The older capability is invalid even if its cryptographic signature remains mathematically correct. Industry equivalents include: secure state lookup,trusted state transition,monotonic counter check,policy epoch check,anti-replay state update, etc. 9. Protected-State Representation The protected-state representation identifies: Which security state did the authorization decision depend upon? For example: epoch = 91 policy_version = 7 revocation_generation = 22 nonce_counter = 1433 quota_state = 4 The representation may alternatively be a cryptographic digest or protected reference identifying that state. The important property is that the authorization decision cannot later become detached from the state under which it was made. In conventional terminology: protected-state representation ≈ trusted state snapshot / state version / state digest / security epoch representation. 10. Protected Validation Evidence Protected validation evidence is evidence that: the relevant predicates were actually evaluated and they were evaluated against a particular protected state. For example: act_digest = H(ACT) policy_version = 7 epoch = 91 decision = ALLOW timestamp = T validation_digest = H(...) MAC/signature = ... Industry terminology may include: authorization decision record,tamper-evident audit evidence,signed validation result,attestation evidence, orcryptographically protected decision receipt. An important aspect of the claim is the ordering: evidence must be committed before, or atomically with, making the capability available. This resembles transactional ordering and commit semantics. It prevents a sequence such as: issue authorization first → maybe record evidence later from satisfying the claimed sequence. 11. Scoped Non-Bearer Capability The expression scoped non-bearer capability combines several established concepts. Capability A capability is an artifact representing permission to perform an operation. Scoped The capability cannot authorize arbitrary operations. For example: SEND X → B does not authorize: SEND Y → C Non-Bearer Simply possessing or copying the capability should not by itself be sufficient to exercise it. A conventional bearer token behaves conceptually like: “Whoever holds this token can use it.” The claim requires something closer to: “This artifact is usable only for this exact act, at this intended sink and boundary, under these specified conditions.” Closest existing terminology includes: proof-of-possession authorization,sender-constrained token,object capability,transaction-specific capability,bound authorization token. However, the claim binds significantly more execution context than is ordinarily implied merely by the phrase “sender-constrained token.” 12. What Is Bound into the Capability? The capability is bound to multiple elements. Candidate Act Meaning: not some other operation. Act Descriptor Meaning: not substituted parameters. Validation Evidence Meaning: tied to the actual protected validation decision. Protected State Meaning: tied to the security state against which authorization occurred. Execution-Finality Boundary Meaning: tied to the intended consequence boundary. Finality Sink Meaning: another enforcement point cannot necessarily exercise the capability. Freshness Meaning: the capability cannot simply remain usable indefinitely. Effectuation Scope Meaning: the capability authorizes only the specified class or range of consequences. In conventional cryptographic and security terminology, this may be described as: cryptographic parameter binding + context binding + channel/resource binding + transaction binding + freshness binding. 13. Capability-Validity Check At the Finality Sink, the system verifies the capability. Such verification may include: verify MAC/signature verify act digest verify sink identity verify boundary identity verify freshness verify nonce verify generation verify revocation state verify scope verify evidence digest verify protected-state reference verify not previously consumed Accordingly: machine-enforced capability-validity check ≈ final policy-enforcement or capability/token-validation procedure. The distinguishing architectural point is where the validation occurs: immediately before the controlled effect. 14. External Effectuation External effectuation means: the operation actually causes its intended side effect. It does not necessarily mean “external to the computer.” For these claims, the relevant effect may include: network transmissionpersistent storage commitmemory modificationDMA transactionaccelerator egressRF emissionoptical transmissionmotor movementpower switching Accordingly, a more conventional engineering description is: externally consequential or protected state-changing side effect. 15. Fail Closed Fail closed is established cybersecurity terminology. The architecture specifies that if an important authorization or verification condition cannot be established, the operation does not proceed. Conceptually: VALID → may effectuate INVALID → deny MISSING → deny STALE → deny REVOKED → deny REPLAYED → deny UNKNOWN → deny UNVERIFIABLE → deny TIMEOUT → deny This corresponds to: default deny / fail secure. It differs from architectures that permit execution when authorization infrastructure, current policy state, or relevant validation information is unavailable. 16. Exhausted Exhausted means that an authorization resource has already been consumed or has reached its permitted use limit. For example: Capability permits one SEND. SEND #1 → permitted Capability marked consumed. SEND #2 → exhausted → denied. Conventional terminology includes: single-use capability,spent authorization, orconsumed token. 17. Indeterminate An indeterminate state exists when the system cannot reliably establish whether authorization remains valid. For example: revocation database reachable? policy version correct? counter synchronized? authorization state valid? The claim treats: UNKNOWN differently from: VALID and therefore requires: UNKNOWN → no effectuation This corresponds closely to: indeterminate policy decision → deny. What Claim 2A Means Claim 2A identifies possible implementations of the Finality Sink for digital or computational side effects. For example: Network-interface controller / DPU / programmable NIC The enforcement point can stop bytes before they physically or logically leave the trusted machine or controlled environment. Memory-controller / memory-commit interface The enforcement point can stop a protected state change before the memory transaction commits. Storage-controller commit interface The enforcement point can prevent persistent data modification until the required authorization has been validated. DMA commit interface The enforcement point can prevent unauthorized direct-memory transfers. Accelerator egress interface The enforcement point can prevent GPU, NPU, or other AI-accelerator output from leaving the controlled computation domain. Accordingly, Claim 2A can be summarized functionally as: Place the reference monitor or enforcement gate at the actual digital side-effect interface. What Claim 2B Means Claim 2B applies the same architecture to the physical and control-system domain. For example: RF Transmit Interface The enforcement point controls whether radio-frequency energy is actually transmitted. Beamforming-Control Interface The enforcement point can prevent an antenna array from generating or emitting the commanded beam. Motor-Control Interface Software may calculate: MOVE MOTOR 30° but the motor does not move until the relevant enforcement point releases the command. Propulsion-Control Interface An AI or control system may determine: THRUST but generation of that computational decision does not itself constitute authority to physically produce thrust. This corresponds to safety and control-system concepts such as: command gating / actuation interlock / safety interlock at the physical output boundary. End-to-End Industry Example Consider a SEND operation: AI system proposes SEND File X to Destination B. Ordinary high-level authorization may resemble: AI → OAuth/IAM authorization → application → SEND The claimed architecture is more like: AI proposes SEND X→B ↓ Hold the SEND Nothing leaves yet. ↓ Create canonical transaction descriptor SEND file = X destination = B account = A purpose = P ↓ Trusted enforcement environment validates authority ↓ Trusted enforcement environment checks protected security state Examples include: revocation, epoch, nonce, quota, policy version, generation state, etc. ↓ Commit protected validation evidence For example: “This exact SEND was validated against protected state S.” ↓ Generate scoped non-bearer capability Bound to: SEND X→B evidence E state S sink F boundary Z freshness T scope P ↓ Finality Sink at NIC/DPU Egress The enforcement point reconstructs or checks what is actually about to leave. ↓ The actual operation is compared against the bound capability. ↓ If all required conditions correspond: Transmit If any required condition does not correspond: Do Not Transmit This expresses the architecture in conventional engineering terms while preserving the distinction between authorization upstream and enforcement at the actual consequence boundary. candidates.title: Hardware-Rooted Protected Execution-Finality Using Scoped Non-Bearer Capabilities and Fail-Closed Finality Sinks
candidates.description: Detailed abstract A hardware-rooted or cryptographically enforced method and system prevent a proposed operation from producing an external effect until that exact operation is validated, bound, and admitted at a non-bypassable effectuation boundary. The proposed operation is first held as a Candidate Act in a non-effective hold state. A machine-verifiable act descriptor is established for the Candidate Act. Within a protected enforcement domain or protected enforcement path—such as a trusted execution environment, hardware security module, secure element, secure processor, SmartNIC, data-processing unit, memory controller, or other isolated circuitry—a set of machine-verifiable authority predicates is evaluated from the descriptor. A corresponding protected-state operation is performed, producing or referencing a protected-state representation. Protected validation evidence recording at least the predicate-validation outcome and the protected-state condition is committed before, or atomically with, authorization of a scoped non-bearer capability. The scoped non-bearer capability is cryptographically or machine-verifiably bound to the Candidate Act, the act descriptor or a digest thereof, the committed validation evidence, the protected-state representation, the execution-finality boundary, an applicable Finality Sink, a freshness constraint, and a permitted effectuation scope. Possession of the capability alone is insufficient: it is not a bearer token, API key, OAuth token, session cookie, or transferable credential. A copied, replayed, substituted, or re-presented instance fails when used for a different act, digest, sink, nonce, policy epoch, protected state, or scope. At or before the execution-finality boundary, the Finality Sink performs a machine-enforced capability-validity check and permits the Candidate Act to become externally effective only when the capability is validly bound to all required elements. Otherwise the system fails closed and the Candidate Act remains non-effective. The Finality Sink may be implemented as a network-interface egress path, memory-commit or DMA interface, accelerator-egress or tensor-egress gate, RF or optical transmit chain, actuator or motor-control interface, settlement switch, fabric switch, CXL/UCIe transaction admission point, or other hardware-controlled effectuation latch. Dependent embodiments apply the same finality sequence to purpose-bound and tenant-bound computation (Data Control Objects, Computational Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints, runtime behavioral descriptors, Linked Act Verification Records), offline CBDC spend-state consumption, cross-border payment compliance, dual-receipt privacy with sealed lawful-resolution material, AI accelerator tensor and KV-cache egress, agentic tool-calls, radio and ISAC telemetry, satellite and non-terrestrial links, robotic actuation, chiplet and photonic I/O, CXL memory-pool admission, and heterogeneous mesh-fabric transfers. Technical effect: computation, recommendation, or token possession is structurally insufficient to cause settlement, emission, actuation, memory coherency, model egress, or other external consequence. Industry-standard keywords Security architecturetrusted execution environment (TEE); confidential computing; hardware root of trust (HRoT); hardware security module (HSM); secure element; secure enclave; remote attestation; measured boot; reference monitor; complete mediation; capability-based security; least privilege; fail-closed; fail-safe; zero trust; policy enforcement point (PEP); policy decision point (PDP); split-trust; compartment isolation Authorization artifactsnon-bearer capability; act-bound capability; scoped capability; capability token; proof-of-possession; sender-constrained token; audience-restricted token; single-use authorization; nonce; freshness; anti-replay; revocation epoch; policy epoch; monotonic counter; capability consumption; burn-in latch Memory, I/O, and fabricIOMMU; SMMU; DMA remapping; RDMA memory key; PASID; VMID; CXL; CXL Type-3 memory pool; UCIe; chiplet interconnect; cache coherency (MESI/MOESI); coherency directory; memory aperture; poison / RAS; SmartNIC; DPU; SuperNIC; line-rate packet processing AI / acceleratortensor egress; KV-cache; mixture-of-experts (MoE); expert routing; GPU fabric; HBM; MIG partition; transformer engine; distillation / model extraction; runtime behavioral descriptor; algorithmic logic fingerprint (ALF); purpose binding; tenant isolation; confidential GPU Payments and regulated systemscentral bank digital currency (CBDC); offline double-spend prevention; sealed spend state; travel rule; AML/CFT; sanctions screening; dual-receipt privacy; lawful-resolution unsealing; settlement finality Telecom / RF / space6G; AI-RAN; O-RAN xApp/rApp; E2/A1/O1; ISAC; NTN; gNB scheduler; UPF; network slice; beamforming; RIS; sub-THz; optical inter-satellite link; LEO-PNT; sovereign jurisdiction token Cyber-physicalsafety interlock; actuator latch; motion envelope; sim-to-real clamping; emergency-stop dominance From an engineering-language perspective, Claims 1 and 2 describe a recognizable security and control architecture, but they use several architecture-specific labels—especially Candidate Act, Finality Sink, execution-finality boundary, protected validation evidence, and execution finality—instead of terminology that an ordinary cloud, hardware, networking, control-system, or cybersecurity engineer would normally search for. Claim 1 is essentially the method/state-machine version of the architecture. Claim 2 is substantially the same architecture expressed as components and responsibilities. The Overall Claim in Ordinary Engineering Language At the highest level, the claims state: Do not allow a proposed side-effecting operation to happen immediately. Stage it first, describe exactly what is about to happen, verify authorization and protected state in a trusted environment, create protected evidence of that validation, issue an act-specific non-transferable authorization artifact, and then require the component that actually controls the side effect to verify that artifact immediately before allowing the side effect. If anything is missing, stale, replayed, changed, or unverifiable, do nothing. The functional flow is: Proposed operation→ stage / hold it→ canonicalize exact operation parameters→ evaluate authorization conditions→ read/update protected security state→ commit protected decision evidence→ create act-specific capability→ verify capability at actual side-effect boundary→ commit/send/actuate only if verification succeeds That is the engineering meaning underneath the terminology. Translation of the Important Terms Claim terminology How standard is the wording? Conventional industry terminology What it actually means protected execution-finality Largely architecture-specific final enforcement, transactional authorization, side-effect gating, commit authorization, reference-monitor enforcement An operation does not become consequential merely because software computed or authorized it. A final enforcement mechanism decides whether the consequence may actually occur. proposed operation Standard request, command, transaction, operation, action Whatever the system seeks to do: SEND a file, write storage, transmit RF, move a motor, make a payment, expose data, etc. Candidate Act Specialized/coined label pending operation, transaction intent, staged command, proposed request, prepared operation The exact operation that is proposed but has not yet been allowed to produce its consequence. non-effective hold state Descriptive but nonstandard pending state, staged state, pre-commit state, prepare state, quarantine, blocked command state The Candidate Act exists inside the system but cannot yet cause the network send, storage commit, actuator movement, payment, etc. execution-finality boundary Specialized commit boundary, side-effect boundary, irreversible-operation boundary, actuation boundary, egress boundary The logical or physical point where an operation changes from merely proposed or computed into something that actually changes the outside world or persistent system state. machine-verifiable act descriptor Specialized compound expression canonical request representation, command envelope, transaction descriptor, operation manifest, canonical parameter set A deterministic machine-readable description of exactly what is about to happen. machine-verifiable authority predicates Partly conventional authorization predicates, access-control conditions, ABAC rules, policy conditions, authorization constraints Boolean or security conditions that must hold before the operation can proceed. protected enforcement domain Fairly conventional concept TEE, secure enclave, HSM, secure element, trusted computing base, isolated reference monitor A trusted or isolated environment in which security-critical validation occurs so ordinary application code cannot simply rewrite the decision. protected enforcement path Specialized expression for standard concept trusted execution path, secure enforcement path, mediation path, trusted I/O path A protected chain through which the security decision and its enforcement travel. protected-state operation Specialized wording secure state lookup/update, trusted counter operation, policy-state lookup, anti-replay update, quota check Reading or modifying security-sensitive state that ordinary untrusted software should not be able to forge. applicable protected-state representation Specialized state snapshot, policy-state version, epoch, counter state, security-state digest, protected record The particular protected state against which the operation was validated. protected validation evidence Specialized authorization decision record, signed decision evidence, attestation evidence, tamper-evident audit record Protected evidence showing what was checked and what the relevant protected state was when the authorization decision occurred. committed evidence Standard distributed-systems concept durable record, append-only audit entry, transaction commit The validation result is made durable or integrity-protected before the operation is allowed to proceed. scoped non-bearer capability Specialized combination of established concepts sender-constrained capability, proof-of-possession token, object capability, transaction-specific authorization token A machine-verifiable authorization artifact that is useful only for the exact permitted operation and cannot be exercised merely because somebody copied the token. cryptographically bound Standard signed binding, MAC binding, hash binding, authenticated association Cryptography connects the authorization artifact to specific parameters so they cannot be substituted afterward. freshness constraint Standard security concept nonce, timestamp, validity interval, sequence number, monotonic counter, epoch Prevents an old authorization artifact from being reused later. permitted effectuation scope Specialized wording authorization scope, action/resource constraints, transaction scope Defines precisely which consequence the authorization artifact is allowed to cause. Finality Sink Strongly architecture-specific/coined policy enforcement point, reference monitor, command gate, actuation gate, commit gate, egress gate, safety interlock The component controlling the last practical point before the consequence occurs. machine-enforced capability-validity check Descriptive token verification, capability verification, PoP verification, authorization enforcement The Finality Sink independently checks that the authorization artifact is valid before releasing the operation. external effectuation Specialized side effect, output commit, egress, transmission, actuation, externally observable state transition The moment the proposed operation actually causes a consequence. fail closed Fully standard security term default deny, fail secure If verification fails or cannot be completed, the consequence is prevented. replayed Fully standard replay attack An earlier valid authorization or operation is reused. exhausted Somewhat specialized in this context consumed capability, spent nonce, used-once authorization, quota exhausted The authorization was single-use or limited-use and has already been consumed. indeterminate Standard policy/security concept decision unavailable, PDP indeterminate, unverifiable state The system cannot reliably determine whether authorization is valid. The claim requires denial rather than guessing. 1. Candidate Act A Candidate Act is: A fully or sufficiently specified operation that the system intends to perform, but which has not yet been permitted to create its actual consequence. Suppose an AI agent determines that a file should be sent: SEND file financial-report.pdf to partner.example.com An ordinary system may operate approximately as follows: AI decision → API call → network stack → SEND Under the architecture: AI decision→ construct SEND(file_hash=X, destination=partner.example.com, protocol=HTTPS, account=A...) → hold that exact operation as the Candidate Act The operation can therefore be inspected, validated, and bound to authorization before packets actually leave the controlled boundary. In conventional terminology: Candidate Act ≈ staged command / pending transaction / transaction intent / prepared operation. The usefulness of the terminology is that a conventional word such as “request” can sometimes refer to something already transmitted or submitted. Candidate Act expressly identifies a state in which: the operation exists, but its consequence does not yet exist. 2. Non-Effective Hold State The non-effective hold state is the state in which the Candidate Act remains before release. It means: The operation has been computed or prepared, but some mechanism prevents it from yet producing the protected consequence. This resembles the prepare stage in transactional systems. For example: Database UPDATE balance ... The update may have been constructed but is not yet committed. Network A message may have been constructed in memory but not yet transmitted through the NIC. Robot MOVE_ARM(x=20,y=15) The command may have been generated, but the motor-control signal remains inhibited. Accordingly: non-effective hold state ≈ staged / prepared / pre-commit / interlocked state. 3. Execution-Finality Boundary The execution-finality boundary identifies the point separating: something the computer intends to do from something that has actually become consequential. The specific boundary varies by technology. Domain Possible execution-finality boundary Network NIC/DPU transmission or egress Storage persistent write or commit Memory protected memory commit GPU/NPU accelerator output or egress Payment ledger or value-transfer commit Telecom RF transmission Satellite command or actuator interface Robot motor or actuator controller Power system switching or enable interface Data disclosure interface that actually releases protected bytes In conventional systems literature, this may be called the: side-effect boundary, commit point, actuation boundary, egress boundary, or irreversible-operation boundary. The claim generalizes those domain-specific boundaries under a common architectural concept. 4. Finality Sink The Finality Sink is not simply another authorization server. It is the enforcement component controlling the actual consequence. In ordinary industry terminology, depending on the implementation, it may correspond functionally to a: reference monitorpolicy enforcement point (PEP)command gateactuation gatetransaction commit gateegress enforcement pointsafety interlock An important additional condition in the claim is that the Finality Sink must be positioned at or before the execution-finality boundary and must control whether the operation crosses that boundary. That positioning is significant. Consider: Authorization server → AI agent → application → OS → driver → NIC Checking authorization only near the beginning of this chain does not necessarily prove that the same operation eventually reached the NIC unchanged. The claim instead requires a structure effectively resembling: Authorization and protected state↓bound capability↓application↓OS/driver↓ Finality Sink ↓NIC transmission The Finality Sink effectively determines: “Is the exact operation about to be released the same operation that was authorized under the relevant protected state?” That is a more precise functional interpretation of Finality Sink than merely describing it as a policy enforcement point. 5. Machine-Verifiable Act Descriptor The machine-verifiable act descriptor answers: Exactly what operation is being authorized? For a SEND operation, it might represent: operation = SEND source = account-A object_digest = 75AE... destination = partner.example.com protocol = HTTPS purpose = regulatory-report maximum_bytes = 8MB expiry = T The actual encoding may use CBOR, JSON, Protocol Buffers, a canonical binary structure, a digest tree, or another deterministic representation. The important requirement is not the particular format. The important requirement is that the representation be deterministic enough for machines to compare what was authorized with what is actually about to happen. Conventional terminology includes: canonicalized request,transaction descriptor,command envelope,signed request parameters, oroperation manifest. 6. Authority Predicates A predicate is essentially a condition that evaluates to true or false. The claim refers to a: “set of machine-verifiable authority predicates” Such conditions may include: user_role == administrator AND operation == SEND AND destination == approved_destination AND file_classification 0 This corresponds to familiar concepts such as: RBAC conditions,ABAC predicates,policy rules,authorization constraints, orpolicy-decision logic. The wording is broader because authority does not necessarily have to originate from a conventional IAM system. 7. Protected Enforcement Domain The protected enforcement domain is a trusted or isolated environment in which security-critical validation occurs so that ordinary application code cannot freely manipulate the validation process or outcome. Claim 2 expressly provides examples such as: secure processor,trusted execution environment (TEE),hardware security module (HSM),secure element,programmable network interface,data-processing unit (DPU),protected controller, etc. Functionally: Protected Enforcement Domain ≈ isolated trusted computing environment containing critical reference-monitor or policy-enforcement logic. Possible implementations include: Intel TDX/SGX-like environmentsARM TrustZone-type environmentsHSMssmart NICs / DPUssecure elementsmicrocontroller protection domainsisolated hypervisor components The claim therefore does not depend upon one particular vendor implementation. 8. Protected-State Operation The architecture does not rely only on static credentials or static authorization. The protected domain may also read or modify security-sensitive mutable state. Examples include: revocation generationnonce stateanti-replay countersingle-use stateremaining quotacurrent policy versioncurrent authorization epochdevice operating state For example: capability_generation = 47 current_generation = 48 The older capability is invalid even if its cryptographic signature remains mathematically correct. Industry equivalents include: secure state lookup,trusted state transition,monotonic counter check,policy epoch check,anti-replay state update, etc. 9. Protected-State Representation The protected-state representation identifies: Which security state did the authorization decision depend upon? For example: epoch = 91 policy_version = 7 revocation_generation = 22 nonce_counter = 1433 quota_state = 4 The representation may alternatively be a cryptographic digest or protected reference identifying that state. The important property is that the authorization decision cannot later become detached from the state under which it was made. In conventional terminology: protected-state representation ≈ trusted state snapshot / state version / state digest / security epoch representation. 10. Protected Validation Evidence Protected validation evidence is evidence that: the relevant predicates were actually evaluated and they were evaluated against a particular protected state. For example: act_digest = H(ACT) policy_version = 7 epoch = 91 decision = ALLOW timestamp = T validation_digest = H(...) MAC/signature = ... Industry terminology may include: authorization decision record,tamper-evident audit evidence,signed validation result,attestation evidence, orcryptographically protected decision receipt. An important aspect of the claim is the ordering: evidence must be committed before, or atomically with, making the capability available. This resembles transactional ordering and commit semantics. It prevents a sequence such as: issue authorization first → maybe record evidence later from satisfying the claimed sequence. 11. Scoped Non-Bearer Capability The expression scoped non-bearer capability combines several established concepts. Capability A capability is an artifact representing permission to perform an operation. Scoped The capability cannot authorize arbitrary operations. For example: SEND X → B does not authorize: SEND Y → C Non-Bearer Simply possessing or copying the capability should not by itself be sufficient to exercise it. A conventional bearer token behaves conceptually like: “Whoever holds this token can use it.” The claim requires something closer to: “This artifact is usable only for this exact act, at this intended sink and boundary, under these specified conditions.” Closest existing terminology includes: proof-of-possession authorization,sender-constrained token,object capability,transaction-specific capability,bound authorization token. However, the claim binds significantly more execution context than is ordinarily implied merely by the phrase “sender-constrained token.” 12. What Is Bound into the Capability? The capability is bound to multiple elements. Candidate Act Meaning: not some other operation. Act Descriptor Meaning: not substituted parameters. Validation Evidence Meaning: tied to the actual protected validation decision. Protected State Meaning: tied to the security state against which authorization occurred. Execution-Finality Boundary Meaning: tied to the intended consequence boundary. Finality Sink Meaning: another enforcement point cannot necessarily exercise the capability. Freshness Meaning: the capability cannot simply remain usable indefinitely. Effectuation Scope Meaning: the capability authorizes only the specified class or range of consequences. In conventional cryptographic and security terminology, this may be described as: cryptographic parameter binding + context binding + channel/resource binding + transaction binding + freshness binding. 13. Capability-Validity Check At the Finality Sink, the system verifies the capability. Such verification may include: verify MAC/signature verify act digest verify sink identity verify boundary identity verify freshness verify nonce verify generation verify revocation state verify scope verify evidence digest verify protected-state reference verify not previously consumed Accordingly: machine-enforced capability-validity check ≈ final policy-enforcement or capability/token-validation procedure. The distinguishing architectural point is where the validation occurs: immediately before the controlled effect. 14. External Effectuation External effectuation means: the operation actually causes its intended side effect. It does not necessarily mean “external to the computer.” For these claims, the relevant effect may include: network transmissionpersistent storage commitmemory modificationDMA transactionaccelerator egressRF emissionoptical transmissionmotor movementpower switching Accordingly, a more conventional engineering description is: externally consequential or protected state-changing side effect. 15. Fail Closed Fail closed is established cybersecurity terminology. The architecture specifies that if an important authorization or verification condition cannot be established, the operation does not proceed. Conceptually: VALID → may effectuate INVALID → deny MISSING → deny STALE → deny REVOKED → deny REPLAYED → deny UNKNOWN → deny UNVERIFIABLE → deny TIMEOUT → deny This corresponds to: default deny / fail secure. It differs from architectures that permit execution when authorization infrastructure, current policy state, or relevant validation information is unavailable. 16. Exhausted Exhausted means that an authorization resource has already been consumed or has reached its permitted use limit. For example: Capability permits one SEND. SEND #1 → permitted Capability marked consumed. SEND #2 → exhausted → denied. Conventional terminology includes: single-use capability,spent authorization, orconsumed token. 17. Indeterminate An indeterminate state exists when the system cannot reliably establish whether authorization remains valid. For example: revocation database reachable? policy version correct? counter synchronized? authorization state valid? The claim treats: UNKNOWN differently from: VALID and therefore requires: UNKNOWN → no effectuation This corresponds closely to: indeterminate policy decision → deny. What Claim 2A Means Claim 2A identifies possible implementations of the Finality Sink for digital or computational side effects. For example: Network-interface controller / DPU / programmable NIC The enforcement point can stop bytes before they physically or logically leave the trusted machine or controlled environment. Memory-controller / memory-commit interface The enforcement point can stop a protected state change before the memory transaction commits. Storage-controller commit interface The enforcement point can prevent persistent data modification until the required authorization has been validated. DMA commit interface The enforcement point can prevent unauthorized direct-memory transfers. Accelerator egress interface The enforcement point can prevent GPU, NPU, or other AI-accelerator output from leaving the controlled computation domain. Accordingly, Claim 2A can be summarized functionally as: Place the reference monitor or enforcement gate at the actual digital side-effect interface. What Claim 2B Means Claim 2B applies the same architecture to the physical and control-system domain. For example: RF Transmit Interface The enforcement point controls whether radio-frequency energy is actually transmitted. Beamforming-Control Interface The enforcement point can prevent an antenna array from generating or emitting the commanded beam. Motor-Control Interface Software may calculate: MOVE MOTOR 30° but the motor does not move until the relevant enforcement point releases the command. Propulsion-Control Interface An AI or control system may determine: THRUST but generation of that computational decision does not itself constitute authority to physically produce thrust. This corresponds to safety and control-system concepts such as: command gating / actuation interlock / safety interlock at the physical output boundary. End-to-End Industry Example Consider a SEND operation: AI system proposes SEND File X to Destination B. Ordinary high-level authorization may resemble: AI → OAuth/IAM authorization → application → SEND The claimed architecture is more like: AI proposes SEND X→B ↓ Hold the SEND Nothing leaves yet. ↓ Create canonical transaction descriptor SEND file = X destination = B account = A purpose = P ↓ Trusted enforcement environment validates authority ↓ Trusted enforcement environment checks protected security state Examples include: revocation, epoch, nonce, quota, policy version, generation state, etc. ↓ Commit protected validation evidence For example: “This exact SEND was validated against protected state S.” ↓ Generate scoped non-bearer capability Bound to: SEND X→B evidence E state S sink F boundary Z freshness T scope P ↓ Finality Sink at NIC/DPU Egress The enforcement point reconstructs or checks what is actually about to leave. ↓ The actual operation is compared against the bound capability. ↓ If all required conditions correspond: Transmit If any required condition does not correspond: Do Not Transmit This expresses the architecture in conventional engineering terms while preserving the distinction between authorization upstream and enforcement at the actual consequence boundary. candidates.description: Thermal conductivity of ethylene glycol at various temperatures Junjie Chen Contributor: Junjie Chen, ORCID: 0000-0001-5055-4309, E-mail address: komcjj@gmail.com, Department of Energy and Power Engineering, School of Mechanical and Power Engineering, Henan Polytechnic University, 2000 Century Avenue, Jiaozuo, Henan, 454000, P.R. China Ethylene glycol is mainly used for two purposes, as a raw material in the manufacture of polyester fibers and for antifreeze formulations. It is an odorless, colorless, flammable, viscous liquid. Ethylene glycol has a sweet taste, but it is toxic in high concentrations. Ethylene glycol is produced from ethylene, via the intermediate ethylene oxide. Ethylene oxide reacts with water to produce ethylene glycol. This reaction can be catalyzed by either acids or bases, or can occur at neutral pH under elevated temperatures. The highest yields of ethylene glycol occur at acidic or neutral pH with a large excess of water. Under these conditions, ethylene glycol yields of 90 percent can be achieved. The major byproducts are the oligomers diethylene glycol, triethylene glycol, and tetraethylene glycol. The separation of these oligomers and water is energy-intensive. Because the methanol is recycled, only carbon monoxide, hydrogen, and oxygen are consumed. The major use of ethylene glycol is as an antifreeze agent in the coolant in for example, automobiles and air-conditioning systems that either place the chiller or air handlers outside or must cool below the freezing temperature of water. In geothermal heating and cooling systems, ethylene glycol is the fluid that transports heat through the use of a geothermal heat pump. The ethylene glycol either gains energy from the source or dissipates heat to the sink, depending on whether the system is being used for heating or cooling. Pure ethylene glycol has a specific heat capacity about one half that of water. So, while providing freeze protection and an increased boiling point, ethylene glycol lowers the specific heat capacity of water mixtures relative to pure water. The freezing point depression of some mixtures can be explained as a colligative property of solutions but, in highly concentrated mixtures such as the example, deviations from ideal solution behavior are expected due to the influence of intermolecular forces. It's important to note that though pure and distilled water will have a greater specific heat capacity than any mixture of antifreeze and water, commercial antifreezes also typically contain an anti-corrosive additive to prevent pure water from corroding coolant passages in the engine block, cylinder heads, water pump and radiator. There is a difference in the mixing ratio, depending on whether it is ethylene glycol or propylene glycol. The use of ethylene glycol not only depresses the freezing point of aqueous mixtures, but also elevates their boiling point. This results in the operating temperature range for heat-transfer fluids being broadened on both ends of the temperature scale. The increase in boiling temperature is due to pure ethylene glycol having a much higher boiling point and lower vapor pressure than pure water, as is typical with most binary mixtures of volatile liquids. In the plastic industry, ethylene glycol is an important precursor to polyester fibers and resins. Polyethylene terephthalate, used to make plastic bottles for soft drinks, is prepared from ethylene glycol. Ethylene glycol is used in the natural gas industry to remove water vapor from natural gas before further processing.
